newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BHF soars on takeover speculation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BHF soars on takeover speculation.

text.p: Shares in German investment bank BHF-Bank AG jumped more than 16 percent on Friday following a newspaper report that Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG was interested in acquiring it.
But both banks denied they were in talks and major shareholders in BHF also said they did not plan to sell their stakes.
"We are not holding talks with BHF-Bank nor with the major shareholders," Bankgesellschaft said in a statement. "Bankgesellschaft's boards are not considering such a move."

The report in respected daily Boersen-Zeitung said Bankgesellschaft was interested in buying at least 75 percent of BHF-Bank and had held talks with big BHF-Bank shareholders, which include insurer Allianz AG Holding and DG Bank .

That gave a further boost to speculation that Germany's overcrowded banking sector faces consolidation after state-owned Bankgesellschaft announced this week it plans to merge with Norddeutsche Landesbank (NordLB).
Most major banking stocks closed higher.

BHF-Bank's stock leapt to a new year's high of 50 marks in pre-bourse trade, up 7.1 marks or 16.5 percent from Thursday's close. Based on a market capitalisation of about 3.7 billion marks, a 75 percent stake would cost about 2.8 billion marks ($1.6 billion).
But the shares pared gains during the floor session amid a flurry of denials from all parties concerned. They closed at 46.10 marks, up 3.45 marks or eight percent.
Analysts said a takeover by Bankgesellschaft now was unlikely because it would be too busy integrating NordLB in the coming years to be able to merge with a third bank.

"Whether Bankgesellschaft has the time and inclination to buy BHF while getting down to the nitty gritty with NordLB is questionable," said Bryan Crossley, banking analyst at ABN Amroa Hoare Govett in London.
"Besides, BHF earns a lot of its money from operations that would be duplicated anyway, like foreign exchange dealing. Why pay for something you can do yourself?"
But analysts said they could imagine Bankgesellschaft pouncing on BHF in a couple of years, attracted by the latter's strength in investment banking.

BHF, often touted as a prime takeover target, has emerged from a difficult 1996. Its operating profit fell five percent as earnings were hit by a dividend omission from industrial holding group AGIV AG, of which BHF owns just under 50 percent.

One of Germany's 10 largest banks, it is well positioned in the domestic corporate banking scene with good links to the Mittelstand, or medium-sized businesses, and would offer a buyer a good foothold in the German market.
UBS is believed to have taken a look at it and other Swiss and Dutch banks are also regarded as potential predators.
But BHF-Bank on Friday received backing from its shareholders in stressing that its shares were not for sale.
Allianz, which owns 15.2 percent, said it did not plan to sell its stake.
DG Bank, which owns 9.6 percent, said it was not in talks on selling the stake and had not been approached, although it added that it did not regard the stake as a strategic investment.
Insurer Alte Leipziger, which owns 6.9 percent, also said it was not in talks and that any sale would have to be at the intitiative of the bank's management or in cooperation with it.
Other major shareholders are IKB Deutsche Industriebank with four percent, Munich Re with 3.7 percent and Italy's Mediobanca.
The remainder of the capital is widely distributed, with about 15 percent believewd to be in the hands of investment funds, according to Boersen-Zeitung.
($ = 1.702 German Marks)
